source: Battambang Provincial Department of Agriculture and the Cambodia Northwest Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (financial support from the SEILA Programme), Khmer translation of Photpeechon Whayooathdee, "ដំណាំខ្នុរ (Jackfruit)", "Translation Copy No. 4", January 1997 (500 copies printed). This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. text:
This short chapter addresses staking/supporting young jackfruit trees and, separately, supporting heavily laden fruiting branches on mature trees. For newly planted trees, the text recommends staking to keep the young trunk straight and to protect it from wind damage and accidental knocks, describing simple stake-and-tie methods using available local materials, with the tie kept loose enough not to girdle the growing trunk and checked/adjusted periodically as the tree grows.

The chapter also discusses a distinct practical problem specific to jackfruit: because fruit can form directly on the trunk and main branches and grow very large and heavy, mature branches (and sometimes the trunk itself) may need physical bracing or propping to prevent breakage under fruit weight, especially during heavy fruit-set years. The source describes several named support/propping methods (the text lists at least four style variants, referenced as types "ហ្គាចម្រុម," "ចប៉្រ្កូ," "ចង្សន្តៃ," and "អ៊ិវ," representing different traditional propping/tying arrangements — exact renderings of these terms carry some transliteration uncertainty from the scan) used by growers to physically support laden branches, generally using forked wooden props set under the branch or ropes/ties anchored to the trunk or ground.

An accompanying illustration on page 41 shows a grower propping a heavily fruited tree, with the text noting that growers should check and adjust supports as fruit continues to swell and gain weight (the source gives an example figure of 25–30% weight gain during final fruit swelling before ripening), since under-supported branches can split or the whole tree can be pulled over by fruit weight in wind.
